definition:
God's attributes are the Bible's ways of saying what God is like: holy, righteous, faithful, merciful, patient, wise, all-powerful, all-knowing, present everywhere, eternal, and unchanging. They are not parts of God, as though he were assembled from goodness, power, and knowledge the way a wall is built from bricks, and they are not moods that take turns. Each names the whole God from one side. His justice is always a loving justice and his love a just and holy love. Theologians have sorted the attributes in several ways. A common Reformed division separates incommunicable attributes, which belong to God alone (self-existence, infinity, eternity, unchangeableness, presence everywhere), from communicable attributes, which God shares in a creaturely measure with those made in his image (wisdom, goodness, righteousness, faithfulness, love). Other traditions speak of God's greatness and his goodness, or of the perfections of his freedom and his love. The study of who God is treats the basic confession of one Creator; the study of holiness and worship treats how a holy God makes a holy people; this study traces how Scripture discloses God's character.

The Bible's vocabulary is rich. In Hebrew, qadosh, ‘holy’, marks God as set apart in majesty and purity. Tsedeq and tsedaqah, ‘righteousness’, name God's rightness and his faithfulness to what is right, and they often stand beside mishpat, ‘justice’ or ‘judgment’. Chesed, which the BSB renders ‘loving devotion’ and others ‘steadfast love’ or ‘lovingkindness’, is loyal, committed love, most often within a covenant, and no single English word catches it. It frequently pairs with 'emet, ‘faithfulness’ or ‘truth’, the reliability of one whose word holds. Rachum, ‘compassionate’, and channun, ‘gracious’, describe God's tender pity and free favor, and 'erek 'appayim, ‘slow to anger’, is an idiom built on the word for nostrils, picturing anger that takes a long time to flare. In the Greek New Testament, hagios is ‘holy’, dikaiosynē ‘righteousness’, agapē ‘love’, charis ‘grace’, eleos ‘mercy’, makrothymia ‘patience’, sophia ‘wisdom’, and pistos ‘faithful’. Pantokratōr, ‘Almighty’, which the Greek Old Testament used for the Hebrew ‘LORD of Hosts’ and often for Shaddai, appears in the New Testament chiefly in Revelation.
ot:
Genesis shows God's attributes in his acts before it names them. The Creator is wise and powerful, making an ordered world by his word and calling it good. He sees and judges, as in the flood, and he binds himself by promise, as with Noah and Abraham. When Abraham pleads for Sodom he appeals to God's own justice: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). God reveals himself to the patriarchs as “God Almighty” (Genesis 17:1) and “the Eternal God” (Genesis 21:33), and the stories show a God who keeps faith through generations of people who do not.

The center of the Old Testament's teaching on God's character is Exodus 34:6-7. After Israel has worshiped the golden calf, Moses asks to see God's glory, and the LORD passes before him proclaiming, “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.” The setting matters: God describes himself this way to a people who have just broken the covenant. Mercy and justice are named together, and the proportion is telling, loving devotion to a thousand generations and judgment to the third and fourth. This self-description echoes through the rest of the Old Testament more than any other: in Moses' prayer (Numbers 14:18), in Nehemiah's confession (Nehemiah 9:17), in the Psalms (Psalm 86:15; 103:8; 145:8), in Joel's call to repent (Joel 2:13), in Micah's closing praise (Micah 7:18), in Nahum's warning (Nahum 1:3), and, pointedly, in Jonah's complaint that God has been exactly this merciful to Nineveh (Jonah 4:2). Israel learned God's character from God's own words, and quoted them back to him in prayer.

The Law and the historical books add God's holiness, justice, and constancy. Israel must be holy “because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). Moses' song calls God “the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just” (Deuteronomy 32:4), and Balaam says, “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind” (Numbers 23:19). The same tension the church would wrestle with appears in a single chapter: the LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king” (1 Samuel 15:11), and Samuel says that “the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind” (1 Samuel 15:29). The narrator holds both, and readers ever since have had to decide how God's steady character relates to his real response to human choices.

The Psalms and Wisdom books praise the attributes directly. “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; loving devotion and faithfulness go before You” (Psalm 89:14). God is eternal, “from everlasting to everlasting You are God” (Psalm 90:2); he knows the psalmist completely and there is nowhere to escape his presence (Psalm 139:1-12); “His understanding has no limit” (Psalm 147:5); and “The LORD is good to all” (Psalm 145:9). Job, after God speaks from the whirlwind, confesses, “I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted” (Job 42:2).

The prophets press the attributes against Israel's complacency and despair. Isaiah hears the seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), and Isaiah 40 sets the everlasting, unwearied Creator against idols and against exiles who think God has forgotten them. God's thoughts and ways are higher than human ones (Isaiah 55:8-9). Jeremiah hears God ask, “Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?” (Jeremiah 23:24), and confesses, “Nothing is too difficult for You” (Jeremiah 32:17). Hosea shows God's holiness expressed as mercy: “My compassion is stirred,” and “I will not come in wrath,” because “I am God and not man, the Holy One among you” (Hosea 11:8-9). Lamentations, written among the ruins of Jerusalem, holds on to the same character: “great is Your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). Malachi grounds Israel's survival in it: “Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed” (Malachi 3:6).
nt:
Jesus assumes Israel's confession of God's character and sharpens it. The Father is perfect, and his children are to be like him (Matthew 5:48). His goodness is lavish and indiscriminate: “He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good” (Matthew 5:45). “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18). God's knowledge and care reach the sparrow and number the hairs of the head (Matthew 10:29-30), and “with God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26). John's Gospel says the Word made flesh was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and many interpreters hear in the pairing an echo of the loving devotion and faithfulness of Exodus 34:6, the Hebrew chesed and 'emet. On that reading, the character God proclaimed to Moses has now appeared in a human life. The Son is “the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3), so the attributes of God are no longer only described; they are seen in Jesus' compassion on the crowds, his anger at the temple, his patience with his disciples, and his faithfulness to the cross.

The cross is where the New Testament shows God's attributes held together most sharply. Paul writes that God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice “to demonstrate His righteousness,” because in his forbearance he had passed over earlier sins, “so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25-26). God's justice and his mercy do not cancel each other; both are satisfied in one act. “God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8), and he is “rich in mercy” (Ephesians 2:4). Paul ends his long argument about Israel and the nations with wonder at God's wisdom: “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Romans 11:33).

The apostles also state the attributes in short confessions. God's “eternal power and divine nature” are seen in what he has made (Romans 1:20). He needs nothing, “as if He needed anything,” since he gives life and breath to all (Acts 17:25). He is “the King eternal, immortal, and invisible” (1 Timothy 1:17). He “cannot lie” (Titus 1:2), and “if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). Hebrews speaks of “the unchanging nature of His purpose” (Hebrews 6:17), and James of the Father of lights “with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (James 1:17), who “cannot be tempted by evil” (James 1:13). Peter repeats Leviticus, “Be holy, because I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16), and says God's apparent slowness is patience, “not wanting anyone to perish” (2 Peter 3:9). John gives the two shortest statements: “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5), and “God is love” (1 John 4:8), a love defined not by our love for him but by his sending his Son (1 John 4:10).

Revelation closes the canon with worship of God's attributes. The living creatures never stop saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come” (Revelation 4:8), repeating Isaiah's vision and adding God's eternity. The redeemed sing, “Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations” (Revelation 15:3), and the angel of the waters says of God's judgments, “Righteous are You, O Holy One” (Revelation 16:5). The Bible ends where Exodus 34 began, with God known by his character, now seen whole.

keyTexts.why: Abraham appeals to God's own justice as the Judge of all the earth. God's character is the ground of prayer.

God's self-description to Moses after the golden calf: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, yet not clearing the guilty. The Old Testament's most quoted statement of who God is.
God is not a man, that he should lie or change his mind. A foundational text for God's truthfulness and constancy.
God is the Rock, his work perfect and his ways just. His faithfulness and righteousness are named together.
The LORD regrets making Saul king, and Samuel says the Glory of Israel does not change his mind. One chapter holds God's response and his constancy together.
God knows the psalmist completely and is present everywhere, from the heavens to Sheol. The Bible's fullest poem on God's knowledge and presence.
The psalmist quotes Exodus 34 and adds that the LORD is good to all and has compassion on all he has made.
The seraphim cry holy, holy, holy. God's holiness undoes the prophet before it cleanses him.
God's compassion is stirred and he will not destroy Ephraim, because he is God and not man. Holiness shows itself as mercy.
Jonah complains that God is exactly as merciful as Exodus 34 says. God's character reaches Israel's enemies.
Because the LORD does not change, Jacob's descendants are not destroyed. God's constancy is the ground of his people's survival.
The Word made flesh is full of grace and truth and makes the unseen God known. The character proclaimed to Moses appears in a human life.
In the cross God shows himself both just and the one who justifies. His righteousness and his mercy meet in one act.
God cannot be tempted by evil, gives every good gift, and has no change or shifting shadow. His goodness and constancy together.
God is love, and love is defined by his sending his Son as an atoning sacrifice. The New Testament's central statement of God's love.

history:
The early church spoke of God's attributes in the language of Scripture and, increasingly, in the vocabulary of Greek philosophy, which already described the divine as unchanging, without body, and not subject to passions. Second-century apologists such as Justin Martyr used these terms to distinguish the Creator from the gods of the cities. Irenaeus, writing around 180 against Marcion and the Gnostics, insisted that the one God is both good and just, against those who divided a merely just Creator from a merely good Father. Augustine taught that God is simple, not composed of parts, so that God is what he has: he does not possess goodness as a quality he might lose, but is goodness itself. Boethius, in The Consolation of Philosophy (around 524), defined eternity as the complete and simultaneous possession of unending life, a definition that shaped the Western tradition for a millennium.

Medieval theology gave the attributes systematic form. Anselm of Canterbury, in the Proslogion (1077 to 1078), reasoned from God as the being than which nothing greater can be thought to his perfections, and wrestled with how a God who is impassible can be merciful. Thomas Aquinas, in the first part of the Summa Theologiae (begun around 1265), treated in order God's simplicity, perfection, goodness, infinity, presence everywhere, immutability, eternity, and unity, then his knowledge, will, love, justice, mercy, and power, and taught that human words apply to God by analogy, truly but not in the same way they apply to creatures. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed one God, eternal, immeasurable, unchangeable, incomprehensible, almighty, and ineffable.

The Reformers received this doctrine and tied it closely to Scripture and to comfort. Calvin, in the Institutes (final edition 1559), cautioned against speculation about what God is in himself and pointed to Exodus 34 and Jeremiah 9:24 as texts that describe God as he is toward us. Reformed and Lutheran scholastics of the seventeenth century developed the distinction between incommunicable and communicable attributes. The Westminster Confession (1646) describes God as infinite in being and perfection, a most pure spirit, without body, parts, or passions, immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, most wise, most holy, most free, and also most loving, gracious, merciful, and long-suffering, and its Shorter Catechism (1647) compressed this into a single answer that generations memorized. Stephen Charnock's Discourses upon the Existence and Attributes of God, published after his death in 1682, remains a classic Puritan treatment.

In the modern period Friedrich Schleiermacher treated the attributes as ways the religious consciousness relates to God rather than descriptions of God in himself. Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/1 (1940), organized them as the perfections of God's loving and of his freedom, insisting that they be learned from God's self-revelation in Christ. The twentieth century saw sustained challenges to impassibility and timeless eternity, from process theology, from Jürgen Moltmann's The Crucified God (1972), and from analytic philosophers of religion, and in recent decades a vigorous retrieval of classical theism in response. The site's full survey is at /theology/doctrine/divine-attributes, and the question of whether God suffers has its own treatment at /theology/doctrine/impassibility.

differ.body: God is simple (not composed of parts), immutable in his being and character, timelessly eternal, and impassible, meaning he is not acted on or overcome by passions as creatures are. Defenders from Augustine and Aquinas through the Reformed and Lutheran confessions, and recent writers such as Paul Helm and Thomas Weinandy, argue that only such a God is truly Creator rather than one more being within the world, and that texts like Malachi 3:6, James 1:17, and Numbers 23:19 teach it. Scripture's language of God's regret or grief is true but accommodated speech, fitted to human understanding like the language of God's arm or eyes. Impassibility does not mean God is unfeeling: he has love, joy, and hatred of evil perfectly and without change, and it is precisely his constancy that makes his love reliable.

God has no beginning or end and is not limited by time as creatures are, but his eternity is best understood as endless duration in which he genuinely acts, responds, and experiences sequence, not as a timeless present. Nicholas Wolterstorff argued this in his essay God Everlasting (1975), and William Lane Craig holds a combined view in which God is timeless without creation and temporal since creating. Defenders argue that the Bible's God speaks, waits, hears prayers, and acts in history, and that a God who knows what time it is now must in some sense be in time. They affirm God's unchanging character and faithfulness fully while holding that strict simplicity and timelessness owe more to Greek philosophy than to Scripture.

God genuinely suffers, not from weakness but from love freely chosen: he grieves over sin and is moved by his people's affliction. Defenders such as Kazoh Kitamori (Theology of the Pain of God, 1946) and Jürgen Moltmann (The Crucified God, 1972), along with many recent evangelical and mainline writers, point to texts like Genesis 6:6, Isaiah 63:9 (“In all their distress, He too was afflicted,” though its Hebrew can also be read another way), and Hosea 11:8, and above all to the cross. They argue that a God who cannot be affected cannot love in the biblical sense, and that the classical doctrine read Scripture through philosophy. Most passibilists still hold that God's suffering never overcomes him or changes his character.

errors:
The church has rejected several distortions of God's character. The oldest sets God's attributes against each other. Marcion in the second century divided a just Creator from a loving Father, and his pattern survives wherever the God of the Old Testament is imagined as wrathful and the God of Jesus as merely kind. Scripture gives the same character in both testaments: Exodus 34 is full of mercy, and Revelation is full of judgment. A related error treats love as God's only real attribute and the others as optional, so that holiness and justice fade into indulgence; the opposite error makes God pure power or pure justice, a will without goodness, whom no one could trust. The Bible's God is holy love and loving holiness at once.

Other errors shrink God. Some make him finite, limited in power or knowledge in the way creatures are, or dependent on the world for what he is. Others treat his power as a tool, as when prosperity teaching makes God's might and generosity a guarantee of health and wealth for those who ask rightly; this mistakes God's faithfulness to his promises for a promise he never made. Still others imagine God as a very large human being, with human moods and human limits, reading the Bible's descriptions of his arm, his eyes, or his regret as if God were simply one of us. The church has held that such language is true but must be read in the light of the whole of Scripture, which says, “I am God and not man” (Hosea 11:9).
life:
What a person believes about God's character shapes everything else. Someone who believes God is powerful but not quite good will obey out of fear; someone who believes he is good but not quite able will pray without hope. Scripture holds the attributes together so that a person can trust God's power because it is always the power of his goodness, and rely on his love because it is always holy, wise, and faithful. The attributes also form the people who know them: Israel was to be holy because God is holy, and Jesus told his hearers to be merciful as their Father is merciful (Luke 6:36).

The attributes are also the substance of prayer. Moses, Nehemiah, the psalmists, Joel, and Jonah all prayed by quoting God's own description of himself back to him, and Christians still do. In grief, God's faithfulness is the reason to keep speaking to him; in guilt, his mercy is the reason to return; in confusion, his wisdom is the reason to wait. Christian hope rests on the same character: the God who does not change and cannot lie will keep what he has promised.
questions: Exodus 34:6-7 names God's mercy and his justice together, and describes God this way to a people who have just broken the covenant. Why does the setting matter for understanding the words?
First Samuel 15 says both that the LORD regretted making Saul king and that he does not change his mind. How do different Christian traditions hold these two statements together?
Which of God's attributes do you find easiest to believe, and which hardest? What might your answer show about the picture of God you actually live by?
